title: Camp 2 close: the story you're in
hook: parables, a birth, a road, a cross, an empty tomb, a church on the move

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc at Rouen. Your line was I am not afraid. Today, the last of the stories.

Seventy-five days of stories. A farmer sowing on every kind of ground. A woman sweeping the house for one coin. A servant who buried his talent because he was afraid. A young woman in Nazareth saying, let it be. A feeding trough. Shepherds on the night shift. Fishermen told to put out into the deep. A short man up a tree. A king on a donkey. A towel and a basin. A rooster. A cross. A garden, and a name said kindly. Then a road to Emmaus, a charcoal fire, wind and flame, a jailer, a shipwreck, a letter full of names. And saints: a mother's tears, a garden in Milan, birds, a wagon in the rain, a girl in armor.
screen: `SEED, COIN, TALENT.` → `A TROUGH, A CROSS, A GARDEN.` → `A FIRE, A FLAME, A SHIPWRECK.`

segments.voice: Mark's Gospel, the shortest, begins, in the King James Bible: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The beginning. Gospel is the old English godspel, good news, translating the Greek euangelion. The Gospels tell it as a story, not a list of ideas: parables that turn things upside down, a birth in the wrong place, a road through Galilee, one last week in Jerusalem, a cross, and an empty tomb. And the book of Acts, where this camp has lived for weeks, doesn't end. Its last scene: Paul under house arrest in Rome two whole years, welcoming all who came, teaching, in the King James words, "with all confidence, no man forbidding him." Then Luke stops. Acts never tells Paul's trial or his death. Some readers take that open ending as deliberate: the story keeps going. Through Stephen and Philip and Lydia, then Monica and Augustine, Francis, Teresa, Joan, and names nobody wrote down. Christians say every life that takes it up becomes another page. That doesn't mean anyone here has to believe it. Some of you walk this path because it's your faith, some because it's someone else's you love, some just to understand. You've walked its length now, from the sower to the shipwreck. Next, this path moves from stories to practices: how Christians pray, sing, rest and live it, day to day. Camp three begins tomorrow. You're in the story now.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `ACTS LEAVES THE STORY OPEN.` · `ANOTHER PAGE, AND ANOTHER.` · `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICES.` · then, large: `YOU'RE IN THE STORY NOW.`

segments.voice: Take the first story from this camp that comes to mind, and ask where it touches your life: the lost coin, the one up the tree, the road to Emmaus, sad, not recognizing something beside you. Find one sentence that says it, and write it down if you can; if you pray, offer it to God.

Euangelion. Greek for good news; old English godspel, gospel. Parable, leaven, talent, annunciation, Magnificat, manger, baptism, disciple, the keys, transfiguration, hosanna, Pentecost, martyr, conversion, Gentile, epistle, agape, saint.
Your line: you're in the story now. Tomorrow, camp three: what prayer is. Camp two, done.

howItsDone: Christians retell these stories every year through the church calendar, from the annunciation and Christmas through Holy Week, Easter and Pentecost, and remember the saints on their feast days. Many churches read the Gospels and Acts in order across the year.

what a scholar hears: euangelion was a word for public good news, like a victory announcement; Acts 28 ends without Paul's trial, and scholars still debate why.
